subtitle: Squeeze a pile of numbers into two or three, then learn the few rules that govern chance, and why a positive test is usually less alarming than it sounds.

center.body:
Suppose someone hands you a thousand exam marks and asks, “So, how did the class do?” You cannot recite a thousand numbers. You need to squeeze them into two or three. The mean x̄ = Σx/n balances the data; the median is the middle value and ignores outliers; the mode is the most frequent.

But averages alone are not enough, because two classes can share a mean and look completely different. So we also measure spread: the variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1) and its root, the standard deviation s, in the same units as the data. Try it on 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. Mean = 40/8 = 5. Squared deviations: 9,1,1,1,0,0,4,16 sum to 32. Divide by n − 1 = 7: s² = 32/7 ≈ 4.57, and s ≈ 2.14. For charts, a histogram shows shape, a box plot shows median and quartiles, and a scatter plot shows pairs. Incomes of 20, 22, 25, 27 and 400 (thousand)? The median describes a typical person; the 400 drags the mean far away.
keynotes: The mean x̄ = Σx/n balances the data, the median is the middle value and ignores outliers, and the mode is the most frequent.
Variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1) and its root s, the standard deviation, measure spread in the same units as the data.

prob.body:
Chance has a grammar, and it has only a few rules. P(A) lies in [0, 1]; the certain event has P = 1. Complement: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A). Addition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Conditional: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). For counting: n! orderings, ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!, ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!).

Roll two fair dice. P(sum = 7): 6 of the 36 outcomes, so 6/36. Now suppose you learn the first die is 3: only (3,4) works, so 1 of 6. Learning something changed the probability, and that is what conditional means. Test yourself: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Is P(A)P(B) = 0.2? Yes, so A and B are independent.
keynotes: P(A) lies in [0, 1]; the complement is P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A); addition is P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), and events are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
For two fair dice P(sum = 7) = 6/36, and given the first die is 3 it is 1 of 6.

bayes.body:
Here is a puzzle that fools doctors: a disease affects 1% of people, and a test is 90% accurate. You test positive. Are you probably sick? Surprisingly, no. Bayes’ theorem reverses a condition: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A)/P(B). The easiest way to use it is to imagine 1000 people.

The disease has prior 1%; the test catches 90% of cases (sensitivity) and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people (specificity 91%). Of 10 sick, 9 test positive; of 990 healthy, 89.1 also do. A positive result therefore means only 0.0917 probability of disease: 9 / (9 + 89.1). Most positives are false alarms because the condition is rare. Raise the prior to 10% in the second figure and the same test is far more convincing. Why a higher posterior with the same test? Because there are now many more truly sick people among the positives.
keynotes: Bayes’ theorem: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A)/P(B); imagine 1000 people to use it.
With a 1% prior, 90% sensitivity and 9% false flags, 9 of 10 sick test positive and 89.1 of 990 healthy do, so a positive result means only 0.0917 probability of disease.
Most positives are false alarms because the condition is rare; raising the prior to 10% makes the same test far more convincing.

mc.body:
When the maths gets awkward, you can let the computer do the thinking. If P(event) is hard to derive, generate many random trials and count. Throwing random points in a unit square and counting those inside the quarter-circle estimates π/4. This run gives π ≈ 3.33 (error 0.1884).

Here is the catch: the error shrinks like 1/√n, so 100× more trials gives only 10× more accuracy. To cut a Monte Carlo error by 10× you need about 100× more trials. Mint points are inside the circle in the figure.
keynotes: If P(event) is awkward to derive, generate many random trials and count.
Random points in a unit square inside the quarter-circle estimate π/4; this run gives π ≈ 3.33 with error 0.1884.
The error shrinks like 1/√n, so 100× more trials gives only 10× more accuracy.

shape.body: How do you read a distribution at a glance? Sort the data first. Q1, the median Q2 and Q3 cut it into quarters; the IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures spread robustly, and points beyond 1.5·IQR from the box are flagged as outliers. And look at the shape: a histogram that trails right is right-skewed (mean > median), as incomes are; a symmetric one has mean ≈ median. In a right-skewed sample, then, the mean is greater than the median.
keynotes: Q1, the median Q2 and Q3 cut sorted data into quarters; the IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures spread robustly.
Points beyond 1.5·IQR from the box are flagged as outliers.
A histogram that trails right is right-skewed (mean > median), as incomes are; a symmetric one has mean ≈ median.

expect.body:
If you play a game thousands of times, what do you win on average? That long-run average is the expectation. A random variable X assigns a number to each outcome. E[X] = Σx·P(x) is the long-run average and Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².

For a fair die E = 3.5. Compute the variance: E[X²] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 15.17, then subtract 3.5² = 12.25, so Var = 2.92 (it is exactly 35/12). Two rules make life easy: linearity E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X); and for independent X, Y, Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y. So if Var(X) = 4, then Var(3X + 1) = 9 × 4 = 36.
keynotes: E[X] = Σx·P(x) is the long-run average and Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².
For a fair die E = 3.5 and Var = 35/12 ≈ 2.92.
E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X); for independent X and Y, Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y.
